slides.title: Find your spot and sit.
slides.notes: Students arrive and choose where to sit. Say: "Find a spot and sit. Where you sit decides how you'll help save the world today."

slides.title: Today looks like this:
slides.notes: Quick roadmap, about 20 seconds. Four things: why we should care, what we do, who we are, and how today works.

slides.title: How many new clothes does the average Australian buy in a year?
slides.notes: Ask the question. Students vote with a hand held up: closed fist = fewer than 10, one finger = about 10, two fingers = about 20, and so on; five fingers = 50 or more. Count to three and everyone shows at once. Look around the room, then click for the reveal.

Reveal 56. Pause. "Who guessed close?" Give a cheer for the nearest. That is more than one new item a week.

ANIMATION (optional): zoom or fade in the 56 on click.

slides.title: So where does it all end up?
slides.notes:
"56 new things a year has to go somewhere." Over 200,000 tonnes of clothing go to landfill each year in Australia (Australian Fashion Council; Seamless reports 222,000 t for 2023). About 23 kg per person discarded (University of Queensland). Many items are worn around 7 times (Baptist World Aid Ethical Fashion Report).

Hand-over: "So what could we do instead? That is what we do."

slides.title: Circular fashion: keep clothes in use
slides.notes:
Bridge from the problem to what we do. A circular approach keeps clothes in use for as long as possible, in this order: reduce, repair, reuse, remake, and recycle last. Mixed materials are hard to recycle because they are joined together and hard to separate. Unstitch sits on reuse and remake: the tiles come apart so they can be used again. Today you practise that part of the ladder.

Timing: about 30 seconds. If the introduction runs long, shorten Who we are.

slides.title: Unstitch: fabric tiles you can build, take apart and remake
slides.notes: Lead on from landfill and the ladder. Introduce the tiles: hold up a real tile or the kit, and connect and disconnect it (no sewing, no stitching). Name four ideas: modularity (tiles combine into larger structures), reversibility (connections can be undone without adhesives or damage), adaptability (the same tiles can be rearranged into different outcomes) and material efficiency (existing components are reused and reconfigured). The fifth idea, thinking by making, comes on the challenge slide.

slides.title: Who we are
slides.notes: Keep it short and personal: how you started, why fabric, what you hope they feel today.

slides.title: The challenge
slides.notes: Read the challenge aloud, then introduce the three words: Rethink. Reuse. Recreate. Introduce the fifth idea, thinking by making: we rethink, reuse and recreate by building, not only discussing. Next: who is on the team.

slides.title: Meet your design team
slides.notes: Designer: leads the idea exploration so the team builds something with a clear user and purpose.

slides.title: Meet your design team
slides.notes: Material Keeper: looks after the tiles, making sure they are in good condition and can be reused as much as possible.

slides.title: Meet your design team
slides.notes: Builder: builds the design and makes sure it holds together and is stable.

slides.title: Meet your design team
slides.notes: Tech Wizard: tries configurations in the playground and brings the best ideas to the team.

slides.title: Meet your design team
slides.notes:
Storyteller: keeps track of decisions, includes everyone and prepares the show and tell.

Wrap up: roles are responsibilities, not exclusive permissions: everyone can build. The role colours (pink, green, coral, blue, yellow) are used only for roles, so students can spot their role on the cards and the hub.

slides.title: What is in your kit
slides.notes:
Go through the kit: tiles, the virtual playground, role cards, the digital brief (on their device, like a sheet of paper), and the starter guide (another sheet of paper).

ANIMATION (optional): make each card appear one by one on click, in this order. Replace the image areas with photos or screenshots.

slides.title: Your three constraints
slides.notes:
These are the three things your design must do. Read them out. Point out the timer in the corner of the projector (part of the hub view).

The three constraints: max 24 tiles; clear purpose and user; adaptable into another configuration.

slides.title: The design loop and the clock
slides.notes:
Read left to right. 15 minutes to explore and build: Design, Make, Construct. A ding (the bell). 10 minutes to test and refine: Iterate, Review. A ding. Last 10 minutes: show and tell (one minute each, bid card), then dismantle and wrap the kit, then reflect. The big dashed loop shows it all returning to Design: circular design, nothing is thrown away.

Suggested dings: after 15: "Time to test. Does it do what you said? Try the virtual playground." After 25: "Wrap up. Show and tell time."

Hand out the kit now. The timer is in the corner of the projector view.

slides.title: Begin the challenge
slides.notes:
Hand out the kits. Read the challenge and the three constraints once. The QR code opens the workshop hub (Participants tab).

The countdown is in the top-right corner of the projector view. Press Start on the hub as you say "Go!".

slides.title: Want to share? Show your bid card
slides.notes: "If your team wants to present, hold up your bid card." Choose 2 to 3 teams. One minute each, covering: our idea, our innovation, our discovery. Keep it moving; applaud each team.

slides.title: Close the loop
slides.notes:
Show the circular loop again, now highlighting the end: share, unbuild, reflect. Close the loop: unbuild the design, wrap the tiles, place the kit on the table. Then reflect and give feedback, in teams or as a class:
- What would you rethink?
- What could you reuse?
- What would you recreate next time?

Next slide: thank you.

slides.title: Thank you!
slides.notes: Thank the students and the school. Then three things they can do this week: wear it more (swap, borrow, buy second-hand), fix or change it (repair, restyle, remake), and ask before you buy (can it come apart, who could use it next?). Link back to the closing question: what would you rethink, reuse or recreate next? Hand back to the teacher.
